title: Biggest Product After Shaving One Off
statement:
You get an array of positive integers nums. Pick two different positions i and j, subtract 1 from each of the two values, and multiply them: (nums[i] − 1) · (nums[j] − 1).

Return the largest product you can get this way. The two positions must differ, but their values may be equal.

examples.why: Take 6 and 4: 5 · 3 = 15. Any pair with the 2 is smaller.
The two 7s sit at different positions, so both may be used: 6 · 6 = 36.
The 3 must be paired with a 1, and 1 − 1 = 0. You cannot pair the 3 with itself.

hints: Every value is at least 1, so both factors are at least 0. Bigger values always give a bigger product.
So the answer only depends on the two largest values. Watch out when the largest value appears twice.
One pass that keeps the largest and second largest values seen so far is enough.

explain.intuition:
Since every value is at least 1, each factor nums[i] − 1 is at least 0, and making either factor larger never makes the product smaller. So the best pair is simply the two largest values in the array, counted by position: if the maximum appears twice, both copies are allowed.

Sorting finds them in O(n log n). A single pass that tracks the top two values does it in O(n), the same way you would track the two highest scores on a leaderboard as rows stream in.
steps: For each value v: if v ≥ first, move first down to second and store v in first.
Otherwise, if v > second, store it in second.
pitfalls: Returning (max − 1)². That pairs the maximum with itself, which is only allowed when it appears twice, as in [3, 1, 1, 1].
Using a strict v > first and then skipping a duplicate maximum, so second never gets the second copy of 7 in [7, 7, 1]. Using ≥ (or the else branch with > second catching the tie) avoids it.

solutions.title: Try every pair
solutions.idea: Check all pairs of different positions and keep the best product.

solutions.title: Sort and take the last two
solutions.idea: After sorting, the two largest values are at the end.

solutions.title: Track the top two in one pass
solutions.idea: Keep the largest and second largest values seen so far.

followups: Values may now be zero or negative and you multiply them without subtracting 1. Which pairs can win now?
Return the k largest products over all pairs. How would a heap help?
lcTitle: Maximum Product of Two Elements in an Array
